qs.q: Anti-nuclear cytoplasmic antibodies can be found in the serum of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a condition that is frequently associated with which other systemic disorder?
qs.e: Anti-nuclear cytoplasmic antibodies can be found in the serum of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, which is characteristically associated with inflammatory bowel disease. This systemic link guides clinical screening in affected individuals.

qs.q: What is the only effective curative therapy for end-stage liver disease resulting from Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis?
qs.e: Liver transplantation is the only effective therapy indicated for end-stage liver disease complications of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Medical therapies like ursodeoxycholic acid are not curative.

qs.q: Which autoimmune inflammatory disease is most commonly associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis?
qs.e: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with autoimmune inflammatory diseases such as chronic ulcerative colitis and Crohn' colitis. It involves non-suppurative inflammation and fibrosis of the biliary ductal system.

qs.q: What is the primary curative therapy indicated for end-stage primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cirrhosis?
qs.e: Liver transplantation is the only effective and life-saving therapy indicated for end-stage liver disease caused by primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cirrhosis. Medical treatments only aim to manage symptoms and slow progression.

qs.q: Which of the following is considered the only effective curative therapy for end-stage primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cirrhosis?
qs.e: Liver transplantation is the only effective and life-saving therapy for end-stage primary sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cirrhosis. Medical therapies only aim to slow disease progression or alleviate symptoms.

qs.q: A patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis develops classic clinical features of cholangitis such as fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice. What does this presentation strongly suggest has occurred?
o: The biliary system has been instrumented
Progression to cirrhosis has spontaneously occurred
qs.e: Clinical features of cholangitis are uncommon in primary sclerosing cholangitis unless the biliary system has been instrumented. Spontaneous cholangitis without instrumentation is rarely the primary presentation.

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) develops jaundice and an intrahepatic mass with normal AFP. Which primary liver malignancy is most consistent?
qs.e: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from the bile duct epithelium. Risk factors include PSC, liver flukes, and Caroli disease. AFP is usually normal, but CA 19-9 may be elevated.

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with a history of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) develops jaundice and an intrahepatic mass. His serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level is within the normal range. Which primary liver malignancy is most consistent with this presentation?
qs.e: Cholangiocarcinoma is a bile duct origin tumor associated with PSC and is characterized by a normal AFP level, differentiating it from typical HCC.

es.q: Detail the clinical presentation, etiology, and diagnostic testing for Primary Biliary Cirrhosis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis.
es.m:
- **Primary Biliary Cirrhosis (PBC):** Progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts causing cholestasis, most commonly affecting women in their 40s or 50s.
- **PBC Presentation & Test:** Presents with pruritis with or without jaundice, and xanthelasma in advanced disease; the most accurate blood test is Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA).
- **Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC):** Progressive obliterating fibrosis of intra and extrahepatic ducts, more common in males than females.
- **PSC Associations:** 75% or more cases occur in association with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

es.q: Describe the clinical features, associated conditions, and medical management goals of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC).
es.m:
- **Definition**: Chronic cholestatic biliary disease characterized by non-suppurative inflammation and fibrosis of the biliary ductal system.
- **Associated conditions**: Associated with autoimmune inflammatory diseases like chronic ulcerative colitis and Crohn’ colitis, as well as Riedel thyroiditis and retroperitoneal fibrosis.
- **Presentation**: Most patients present with fatigue, pruritus, and occasionally jaundice; classic cholangitis features are uncommon unless the biliary system is instrumented.
- **Medical management goals**: Because there is no curative medical therapy, goals are to treat symptoms and prevent or treat known complications.

ai.title: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A chronic, immune‑mediated inflammation of intra‑ and extrahepatic bile ducts leading to fibrosis and strictures. It is closely linked to ulcerative colitis and presents with cholestatic liver biochemistry and pruritus.

sections.p: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a progressive cholestatic liver disease characterised by multifocal inflammation and fibrosis of the biliary tree. Diagnosis requires cholestatic biochemistry, characteristic cholangiographic changes and exclusion of other causes.
b: Imaging: MRCP or ERCP shows beaded, strictured ducts; ultrasound may show ductal dilatation
Histology: onion‑skin fibrosis, periductal inflammation; liver biopsy is supportive but not mandatory

t.b: Is the patient cholestatic? A level >2× upper limit suggests cholestasis.
Shows beaded appearance of bile ducts; confirms PSC when typical.
Provides histologic confirmation of periductal fibrosis; useful if imaging is inconclusive.

sections.p: Staging is based on Mayo Risk Score and imaging severity. Early disease may be asymptomatic; advanced disease leads to cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
b: Mayo Score: age, bilirubin, AST, albumin, INR; higher score predicts mortality.

t.b: Predicts 5‑year survival; a score >3 indicates high risk.

sections.p: PSC is idiopathic but strongly associated with ulcerative colitis and other autoimmune conditions. In low‑resource settings, infections such as hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, and herbal hepatotoxins may mimic or exacerbate PSC.

t.b: Rules out viral hepatitis as cause of cholestasis.
Detects schistosomal infection that can cause biliary strictures.

sections.p: Patients often report pruritus, fatigue, and painless jaundice. Physical exam may reveal jaundice, hepatomegaly, and rarely, palpable gallbladder. In advanced stages, splenomegaly and ascites appear.

t.b: Assesses impact on quality of life; guides need for bile acid sequestrants.

sections.p: A stepwise approach is essential, prioritising tests that are affordable in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects anemia or thrombocytopenia indicating portal hypertension.
Confirm cholestatic pattern; rising bilirubin suggests progression.
Rules out IgG4‑related cholangitis, which mimics PSC.
Initial imaging to assess ductal dilatation and exclude gallstones.
Gold standard for ductal morphology; if unavailable, ERCP can be used.
Excludes viral hepatitis.
Support diagnosis of associated autoimmune disease.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents morbidity. Watch for signs of cirrhosis, cholangiocarcinoma, and portal hypertension.
b: Portal hypertension: ascites, variceal bleeding, splenomegaly
Cholangiocarcinoma: new jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain

t.b: Detects esophageal varices; bleeding is a medical emergency.
Identifies mass lesions suggestive of cholangiocarcinoma.

sections.p: Treatment focuses on symptom control, surveillance, and addressing underlying causes. No curative medical therapy exists; liver transplantation is definitive for end‑stage disease.

t.b: Reduces pruritus by binding bile acids in the gut.
May improve liver biochemistry; use cautiously due to limited evidence.

Indicated when bilirubin >2 mg/dL, MELD >15, or complications arise.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of liver function, imaging, and cancer surveillance is mandatory. Prevention focuses on treating associated UC and avoiding hepatotoxic substances.

Screen for cholangiocarcinoma; elevated levels warrant further imaging.

sections.p: Differential includes IgG4‑related cholangitis, secondary sclerosing cholangitis (post‑infectious, post‑surgical), and biliary atresia in children.

t.b: High levels suggest IgG4‑related disease rather than PSC.
Steroid responsiveness indicates IgG4 disease.

t.b: A normal level does not exclude PSC if clinical suspicion is high.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening jaundice, severe abdominal pain, haematemesis, new ascites, or unexplained weight loss

faq.a: No, but liver transplantation can restore liver function.

faq.q: Is PSC related to hepatitis B?
faq.a: HBV can cause cholestasis but is a separate entity; PSC is autoimmune.

faq.q: What is the best imaging test?
faq.a: MRCP is preferred; ERCP is used if therapeutic intervention is needed.

exam: What is the most specific imaging finding for PSC? — Beaded, strictured intra‑ and extrahepatic ducts on MRCP.
How would you differentiate PSC from IgG4‑related cholangitis? — High serum IgG4 and steroid response favour IgG4 disease.
A patient with PSC develops sudden jaundice and weight loss. What is the next step? — Perform CT abdomen to rule out cholangiocarcinoma.
What drug is first‑line for pruritus in PSC? — Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant.
When is liver transplantation indicated in PSC? — Bilirubin >2 mg/dL, MELD >15, or complications like variceal bleeding.
Why is ursodeoxycholic acid used cautiously in PSC? — Limited evidence of benefit and potential for worsening liver enzymes.
What surveillance test is recommended annually for cholangiocarcinoma in PSC? — MRCP and CA 19‑9/CEA monitoring.
